text: Support for Non-Terrestrial Networks \(NTN\) has been introduced in the 3GPP specifications starting from Release 17. Release 18 has been recently completed, with further enhancements in development as part of Release 19 and expected in the upcoming Release 20.
trace: Introduction
text_preview: Support for Non-Terrestrial Networks \(NTN\) has been introduced in the 3GPP specifications starting from Release 17. Release 18 has been recently completed, with further enhancements in development as part of Release 19 and expected in the upcoming Release 20.

text: NTN has gained substantial momentum in the telecommunication industry, with the first services in support of IoT and directto-device messaging launched, and more deployments including NR-NTN upcoming. NTN presents an emerging opportunity for Open RAN and there are multiple research/development projects and evaluations in progress focusing on NTN implementation leveraging Open RAN technologies. Non-Terrestrial Networks, in particular NGSO constellations, dynamic GSO, as well as hybrid multi-orbit constellations, present complex architectural, control, radio resource management, mobility and orchestration challenges which could be addressed by Open RAN technologies.
trace: Introduction
text_preview: NTN has gained momentum in telecommunication, with IoT and direct-to-device services launched. NTN presents an emerging opportunity for Open RAN, with ongoing research/development projects focusing on its implementation. Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) face complex challenges, including architectural and control issues, which can be addressed by Open RAN technologies.

text: The O-RAN ALLIANCE is currently developing specifications for O-RAN RIC-enabled optimization and autonomous management of terrestrial networks. Standardization of O-RAN RIC-enabled optimization and autonomous management for NTN and converged NTN+TN interworking deployment scenarios is essential for the NTN operator constellation planning and architectural phases, as a key enabler for their commercial success.
trace: Introduction
text_preview: The O-RAN ALLIANCE develops specifications for O-RAN RIC-enabled optimization and autonomous network management. Standardization is crucial for NTN operator constellation planning and architectural phases, enabling commercial success.

text: This intelligent management of the RAN and its operation is naturally addressed by the Non- and Near-RT RICs. However, while there are many use cases documented for their employment in terrestrial 5G networks, moving the network functions into space brings in a whole new set of challenges and constraints, and opens up completely different novel implementation approaches for the existing O-RAN use cases \(such as TS and QoS optimization\), as well as a new host of use cases that are specific to NTN. For example to account for the new control signaling features introduced for NTN in 3GPP Releases 17 and 18 \(such as SIB19 and timer/distance-based CHO\), as well as to address challenges unique to NTNs.

text: 4.1.1 Overview

text: Non-Terrestrial Networks \(NTN\) are a significant focus within the 3GPP standards, particularly for integrating satellite into 5G and beyond. Here's a summary of the current development status:
trace: 4.1 3GPP --> 4.1.1 Overview
text_preview: Non-Terrestrial Networks \(NTN\) are a significant focus within the 3GPP standards, particularly for integrating satellite into 5G and beyond. Here's a summary of the current development status:

text:
* 1\. Release 15 and 16: Study phase on scenarios, use cases, channel models and impact of NTN to the 5G System, as well as solutions for 5G New Radio \(NR\) support for Non-Terrestrial Networks.
  * 2\. Release 17 and 18: These releases introduced NTN with a transparent \(bent-pipe\) architecture, where satellites act as radio repeaters without on-board processing capabilities. This approach was chosen for its simplicity and early deployment potential. Both NR-NTN and IoT-NTN are supported. Release 18 introduced support for NR NTN above 10 GHz, such as broadband in Ka band.
  * 3\. Release 19: This release marks a major milestone with the introduction of a regenerative payload architecture. In this scenario, a complete gNB \(Next Generation Node B\) is placed on the satellite, allowing for greater integration and flexibility, and opening up new constellation topologies and use cases\). This architecture supports packet processing directly on the satellite, enabling features like improved mobility management.
  * 4\. Release 20: The next release is currently in the planning phase and a 3GPP RAN workshop in RAN\#106 \(12/2024\) discussed potential NTN features for Rel-20. The initial work plan for Rel-20 was decided in RAN\#108 \(06/2025\).

text: Technological Challenges: The development of NTN involves unique challenges such as high Doppler shifts, longer propagation delays, and larger cell sizes due to the high altitudes of satellites. Enhanced beam management and regulatory considerations are also crucial. Most of these challenges are already covered by Rel-17 and 18.
trace: 4.1 3GPP --> 4.1.1 Overview

Enhanced beam management and regulatory considerations are also crucial. Most of these challenges are already covered by Rel-17 and 18.

text: Future Prospects: The ongoing work aims to further integrate NTN with terrestrial networks, enhancing global coverage and resilience. The regenerative payload architecture is expected to support advanced functionalities like "store and forward," which allows satellites to store data temporarily and forward it when connectivity is restored, and also UEsatellite-UE communication with reduced latency.

text: In most cases, these NTN networks and services are not anticipated to be completely standalone offerings, but rather intended at least in part as a complement to Terrestrial Networks, for example to provide coverage extension in white spots and hard to reach areas, 3D coverage at altitude, or a layer of resiliency. In fact, the ability for NTN to eliminate or alleviate coverage gaps in the Terrestrial Network was one of the key motivations for the introduction of NTN in 3GPP since the beginning.

Existing Satellite Network Operators (SNOs) expanding into NTN, including:

* Existing SNOs evolving non-3GPP services
* New entrant SNOs offering unique NTN services
* Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) extending their networks via NTN
* New entrant MNOs providing homogenous TN and NTN coverage

text: Therefore, it is expected that many MNOs may seek to extend their own Terrestrial Network services via NTN, however the current market trends indicate that they will likely not seek to deploy and operate their own satellites, but rather form agreements with one or multiple NTN SNOs, who will provide coverage over areas of interest on behalf of their partner MNOs.

text_preview: Many MNOs may extend Terrestrial Network services via NTN, but they're unlikely to deploy and operate their own satellites. Instead, they'll form agreements with NTN SNOs, who will provide coverage in areas of interest on behalf of their partner MNOs.

text: For this to be achieved, the MNO's and SNO's networks will need to interact and coordinate with one another at some level. The required degree of interaction and information sharing required between the two operator domains will depend on the requirements of the specific use case and on the depth of integration between the two segments. This interaction is essential in order to for example make the NTN network aware of where the boundaries of the terrestrial network exist, share handover preparation information, reselection targets, etc. and conversely make the terrestrial network aware of when an NTN is available to its users.

text: 5.1.2.1 Use Case Description

text: In order for an MNO and their partner SNO\(s\) to be able to support efficient complementary coverage via NTN, the TN network may need to be aware of the available NTN coverage footprint, and vice versa. This can include current coverage \(i.e. already active\) as well as potential coverage \(i.e. not yet active, but possible\), and will need to include some details of the coverage to be provided \(e.g. applicable NTN cells, their configuration and corresponding serving satellite ephemeris\).
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.2.1 Use Case Description
text_preview: For MNOs and SNOs to support efficient complementary coverage via NTN, the TN network must be aware of available NTN coverage footprint and vice versa. This includes current (active) and potential (possible) coverage, as well as details on applicable cells, configuration, and serving satellite ephemeris.

text: Depending on a number of operational factors and system constraints, such as feeder link availability, power and radio resource availability of the satellites forming the NTN constellation, the active cells, allocated resources \(and thus capacity\), as well as the specific coverage areas that an NTN operator chooses to serve or not serve may change over time. In addition, due to orbital precession, the specific satellite\(s\) serving a given cell coverage area on the ground at any point of time \(e.g. in a scenario with Earth-fixed or quasi-Earth-fixed Cells\) also change over time. Thus there is a need for the NTN segment to be able to communicate this information to the TN segment, such that the TN segment can be aware of which NTN cells are available or might become available in the future, as well as update the information being broadcast in SIB19/SIB31 messages in terrestrial edge cells.
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.2.1 Use Case Description
text_preview: The NTN constellation's operational factors and system constraints can change due to feeder link availability, satellite power, radio resources, allocated capacity, and coverage areas served. Orbital precession affects specific satellites serving cell coverage areas, impacting communication with TN for updates on available or potentially available cells.

text: Likewise, in the reverse direction, an NTN operator may normally not be aware of the footprint, topology, configuration or even presence of terrestrial networks within the coverage of an NTN, unless this information has been separately sourced or disclosed by the MNO. Whilst some of this information can be shared at network planning by the TN MNO to the NTN SNO,

text: 5.1.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.2.2 Problem statement and challenges

text: In order to fulfil the requirements of these scenarios, the TN and NTN segments would need to have a method of exchanging at least the minimum necessary information on their respective coverage footprints, required to fulfil complementary coverage functionalities. The current 3GPP- and O-RAN-specified interfaces between operator domains, such as the roaming interfaces and other interfaces at the Core network and RAN level \(e.g. Xn\), do not support sharing of this type of information.
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
text_preview: To fulfil requirements, TN and NTN segments need to exchange minimum necessary info on coverage footprints for complementary functionalities. Current 3GPP/O-RAN interfaces don't support this, such as roaming interfaces at Core network & RAN level (e.g. Xn).

text: Sharing of neighbor cell information, including neighbor relationships, and other coverage related information within a single network domain \(e.g. within a TN or an NTN\) is typically expected at least in part to be addressed by interfaces such as X2/Xn. However, in the interaction between TN and NTN this is either not sufficient \(e.g. due to lack of the necessary primitives\), or outright not possible, such as in the scenario where SNO and MNO, with both networks assumed to be aligned with 3GPP and O-RAN architecture, are two distinct operator domains, where inter-operator Xn is currently not contemplated \(or implemented\) and presents potential feasibility issues. In addition, both the TN footprint, topology and configuration, as well as the NTN footprint, topology and configuration, are expected to be continuously evolving and dynamic in nature, especially as operators \(MNOs and SNOs alike\) increasingly target maximization of energy and deployment efficiencies. Therefore, traditional manual or static mechanisms of sharing this information are not going to be fit for purpose, and there is instead a need for automated mechanisms that can dynamically provide updates on the changes to the coverage in a timely manner \(order of seconds at least\), as soon as they happen. It is also important that this sharing of information is performed securely and with a fine-grained level of control on the type and amount of information that is respectively shared, at any given instant of time.

text: This use case covers the support for mobility and service continuity between a terrestrial network \(TN\) and a Non-Terrestrial Network \(NTN\). One of the key value propositions for Non-Terrestrial Networks is to enable complementary coverage for terrestrial networks, and to help MNOs fulfil coverage gaps. As such, enabling or facilitating mobility and service continuity between the TN and the NTN and vice-versa is a key requirement.
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.3 Use Case 1-2: TN-NTN Mobility and Service Continuity --> 5.1.3.1 Use Case Description
text_preview: This use case supports mobility and service continuity between Terrestrial Network (TN) and Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN). Enabling seamless coverage for MNOs, it helps fill coverage gaps by facilitating TN-NTN and NTN-TN connectivity.

text: Whilst 3GPP defines the procedures at RAN level for TN-NTN idle and connected mode mobility and stipulates the need for sharing of coverage and satellite assistance information \(e.g. Ephemeris\), the 3GPP specifications do not explicitly address how this information is shared, and further how these procedures are coordinated when the TN and NTN are in different operator domains. This use case thus describes the requirements, expected procedure and possible solution to address these remaining aspects in respect to TN-NTN mobility and service continuity.
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.3 Use Case 1-2: TN-NTN Mobility and Service Continuity --> 5.1.3.1 Use Case Description
text_preview: 3 gpp defines ran - level procedures for tn - ntn idle and connected mode mobility , including coverage sharing and satellite assistance ( e . g ., ephemeris ). however , specifications don 't address information sharing across different operator domains . this use case outlines requirements , expected procedure , and possible solution to address gaps in tn - ntn mobility

text: In order to be able to support TN-NTN mobility, the TN RAN needs to be aware of the NTN coverage footprint, and specifically which satellite\(s\) are or will be serving a given coverage area at any point in time, and which are or may be the applicable neighbor NTN cells, with their respective configurations. In 3GPP NTN Rel-17+ systems, some of this information, alongside other details such as Ephemeris of the satellites, is expected as per the 3GPP specifications to be delivered via SIB19 or SIB31 into the TN cells bordering or overlapping with the NTN coverage area. However, in order for the information to be delivered to the TN cells, the terrestrial network has to first be aware of the information in the first place. This information may in many cases need to come from an external source to the MNO network \(e.g. an SNO network\). In addition, there may be another scenario in which an MNO may wish to provide

text_preview: Therefore, these challenges arise with this scenario and the lack of a suitable interface, for example:

text:
* No awareness by the TN of the target NTN cell configuration \(e.g. frequencies, PCI, etc\) required to configure measurements, HO triggers, Reselection policies.
  * No awareness of the gNB topology in the target network \(either TN or NTN\), and thus no awareness of which gNB to even establish an Xn connection or trigger an HO request or measurement request.
  * With 3GPP NTN R17+, the TN might not be aware of Satellite Ephemeris \(SIB19/SIB31 content\), required by the UE to perform UL pre-compensation
  * The NTN coverage may not be active \(or may be configured with insufficient duty cycle/capacity\) in the target area that the UEs are about to move to \(satellite coverage is limited and must be selective\)
  * The NTN may not have any awareness of incoming load, QoS requirements or UE capabilities
  * In 3GPP R19 NTN, SSB Periodicity could be relaxed \(e.g. up to 160ms\). This can impact UE sync performance/reliability and may need specific SMTC configuration for measurement before TN to NTN handover
  * UE capability signaling is very heavy. Forcing the NTN to perform UE capability exchange from scratch may have adverse impact on NTN capacity
  * Letting the UE/network declare RLF and Detach the UE, would lead to a network selection/access from scratch, which creates service interruption and unnecessary signalling load.
  * The NTN network may not be aware of which \(or any\) UE in TN are about to be handed over \(or reselect to\) NTN

text: In some cases a Terrestrial MNO might wish to explicitly request NTN coverage in a given area, either to fulfil a coverage gap, or to respond to a total or partial outage of the terrestrial network, such as in a disaster scenario. This same capability could also be used simply to request the NTN to allocate additional capacity in a given area, in order to respond to an expected or witnessed increase in demand.

text: Scenario 1\) TN MNO1 identifies a coverage gap in its coverage, or is interested in providing additional coverage overlay, and thus requests NTN coverage to specific target geographical area to NTN SNO1.

text: Current methods for an MNO to request NTN coverage from an SNO are entirely reliant on traditional office IT communication \(e.g. emails, meetings\), and require extensive discussions and pre-agreements not only at the commercial level, but also at the technical level, as a pre-requisite.
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.4 Use Case 1-3: Request of NTN coverage for Disaster Response --> 5.1.4.1 Problem Statement
text_preview: Current methods for an MNO to request NTN coverage from an SNO are entirely reliant on traditional office IT communication \(e.g. emails, meetings\), and require extensive discussions and pre-agreements not only at the commercial level, but also at the technical level, as a pre-requisite.

text: With current methods, derivation of technical parameters for requests of either complementary coverage or capacity rely on extensive offline simulations performed by both parties respectively. These simulations are usually based on abstracted knowledge of the network, and relatively limited advance knowledge of the respective systems, also due to confidentiality constraints. From these simulations and plans, a notional NTN network plan is usually derived and agreed by both parties, via extensive discussion. In some cases, the simulations used to derive the plan may not even be fully reflective of the up-to-date conditions of the network \(mostly because they are generated not from the live network, but from offline system-level simulator toolsets\), nor of the real-world practical conditions in which the system will operate.

Simulations are based on abstracted network knowledge and limited advance information due to confidentiality constraints. A notional NTN network plan is derived, but may not reflect up-to-date conditions.

text: In addition, any subsequent update usually needs to go through a similar formal cycle of discussions, simulations, agreements and formal approvals, de-facto preventing the enactment of any reactivity to changing requirements or events in responsive timeframes. In some cases, due to the relatively "static" nature of the plan and of the need to pre-plan in advance, often with a high level of detail, this can also lead to inflexibility in any regulatory filings submitted, where exact static values may be specified or filed for, and thus require an update to the regulatory filings in case some parameters are altered or optimized.

* 1\) Staleness: The NTN network plan derived is relatively static and represents a snapshot of the respective systems at a given moment of time, which may become stale over time, due to being unable to automatically reflect any subsequent changes or optimizations in either the MNO terrestrial network coverage, or the SNO's NTN coverage.
  * 2\) Immutability and lack of reactivity: Changes in the NTN network plan are difficult and slow to introduce, and not only it cannot easily accommodate either changes in the actual respective network topologies, capabilities and plans, but it is also unable to be adapted in responsive time frames, to react to changing or unforeseen needs by either SNO or MNO, such as need to provide Disaster Coverage in response to an outage, spikes in demand or other timesensitive events.
  * 3\) Poor accuracy: Due to the simulation environments used to derive the technical parameters of the plan, and due to issues with confidentiality, the plan may not reflect the accurate and up-to-date state, capabilities or parameters of the live network, reducing the accuracy of representation. Its accuracy also to the physical live environment and its interaction with terrain, weather and other factors is also very limited.
  * 4\) Conservativeness and sub-optimality: Due to the above issues, the plans are usually defined with relatively \(sometimes extremely\) conservative margins, in order to avoid, or at least reduce, any risks of disruption to user experience. Inevitably, this also results in significant sub-optimality.

text: These issues could be resolved via a form of automated and programmatic mechanism, enabling the exchange of requests \(as well as advertisements of availability\) for coverage and capacity between different entities, such as for example between one MNO and one or more SNOs to provide NTN coverage and capacity in reaction to changing demand or to an unforeseen even, such as a disaster scenario.
trace: 5.1.2 Use Case 1-1: TN-NTN Coverage Information Sharing --> 5.1.4 Use Case 1-3: Request of NTN coverage for Disaster Response --> 5.1.4.1 Problem Statement
text_preview: These issues could be resolved via automated mechanisms that enable exchange of requests and availability notifications between entities, such as MNOs and SNOs, for NTN coverage and capacity in response to changing demand or disasters.

text: There are currently no existing interfaces, APIs or otherwise programmatic and/or automated mechanisms to support either static, semi-static or let alone dynamic requests for coverage and/or capacity between different operator entities within either the 3GPP or the O-RAN specifications. Such requirements and concepts have been raised and discussed from time to time, at least within 3GPP in the context of NTN, but have never so far been introduced. In particular, there is currently no satisfactory mechanism to satisfy certain mission-critical use cases for the public good, such as respond to the need to supply Disaster Coverage via NTN in response to total or partial outages to parts or totality of an MNO's terrestrial network within meaningfully responsive timeframes from the occurrence of an event \(e.g. seconds or at most minutes\).

text: In order to satisfy the requirements outlined above, for the scenario in which the TN and NTN segments are operated by different operators, an MNO and an SNO respectively, or under otherwise different administrative domains, a potential proposed solution is the introduction of a new and novel O-RAN interface or API between the two operator domains that is suitably designed to cross the inter-operator domain trust boundary.

text: If we assume that both the TN and NTN are respectively adopting the O-RAN architecture and thus both have their own respective Near/Non-RT RIC and SMO deployments, the new interface could be designed to exist between the MNO's and SNO's respective Near/Non-RT RICs or SMOs, facilitating different levels of information sharing. Such capability and interface are not currently specified or contemplated by the O-RAN Architecture and Specifications, and therefore it is identified as a gap. Overall, this cross-operator mode of operation and interaction was not envisaged by 3GPP or the O-RAN Alliance previously and would require investigation into how the O-RAN architecture may need to evolve, potentially with the specification of one or more new interfaces.

text: This use case covers the use of an NTN near-RT RIC and xApps to optimize the implementation of inter-satellite inter-gNB Connected Mode Handover \(HO\) within an NTN Non-Geostationary Orbit \(NGSO\) constellation, exemplified by a Low Earth Orbit \(LEO\) constellation, driven by satellite mobility. This use case is in principle formulated in a way that is largely agnostic of the NTN gNB architecture \(e.g. Transparent vs Regenerative\). In this scenario, users are assumed to be practically stationary or slow moving \(e.g. handheld\), and the mobility events are driven by satellite motion. This scenario use case description assumes Earth-fixed cells \(EFC\) or quasi-Earth-fixed cells \(QEFC\), but is applicable also to Earth-moving cells \(EMC\).

text: Many upcoming 5G NTN constellations will be deployed in Low Earth Orbit, where a significant number of satellites are needed in order to achieve ubiquitous global coverage. LEO constellations are highly-mobile, and as such UEs may experience frequent handovers from one satellite to the next.

text: In addition, in dense constellations, multiple candidate satellites may be able to serve a given coverage area, introducing the need for the network to select the appropriate target satellite to serve the incoming users. This could be influenced by a number of factors, such as feeder link availability, expected satellite visibility period, maximum number of concurrent beams, on-board power limitations, UE TX power and antenna gain, line of sight, spectrum constraints and more.

text: The first part of the problem statement is relatively trivial. In order to support NR NTN scenarios aligned with 3GPP Release 17 and above, the Near-RT RIC and xApp must be able to configure the required NTN-specific measurement configurations, as well as the necessary handover triggers.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview --> 5.2.2 Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover \(HO\) due to Satellite mobility --> 5.2.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
text_preview: The first part of the problem statement is relatively trivial. In order to support NR NTN scenarios aligned with 3GPP Release 17 and above, the Near-RT RIC and xApp must be able to configure the required NTN-specific measurement configurations, as well as the necessary handover triggers.

text: In Release 17, a new SSB Measurement Timing Configuration \(SMTC\) specific to NR NTN, namely SMTC4 \(SSB-MTC4Listr17\), has been introduced. In addition, the NTN cells must be able to broadcast Satellite Assistance information, in particular Satellite Ephemeris, in the form of SIB19, containing serving and neighbor satellite and cell information. Furthermore, in order to trigger a HO, the gNB must be able to include specific SIB19 content in the HO triggers.

The NTN cells must broadcast Satellite Assistance information, including Satellite Ephemeris, via SIB19. To trigger a Handover (HO), the gNB must include specific SIB19 content in HO triggers.

text: This implicitly requires the NTN Near-RT RIC and xApp\(s\) to be aware of the constellation Ephemeris, the serving and target satellite timing information, as well have the ability to deliver the necessary configurations to the O-CU/DU.

text: The second aspect of the problem is related to coordination of the HO across multiple satellites \(and cells, potentially gNBs\), in order to hand the UE over to the best satellite.

text: Several criteria and KPIs may be taken into account to select the best target satellite, and, depending on the service requirements set by the SNO, the NTN RIC may have to either privilege one or more specific KPIs at the expense of others, or to perform a multi-constraint evaluation by ensuring adequate and balanced satisfaction of several different KPIs at once.

text_preview: To select the best target satellite, various criteria and KPIs are considered. The NTN RIC may prioritize specific KPIs over others or evaluate multiple constraints to balance satisfaction across multiple KPIs.

text: In terrestrial networks, assessment of handover opportunities is almost entirely focused on KPIs affecting the user link, and would typically be driven by UE measuring the SSBs of relevant neighbour cells, and then the gNB or Near-RT RIC monitoring for SMTC-configured measurement events where the quality on a neighbour cell signal would exceed a given threshold, while that of the serving cell would drop below another threshold, such as is the case in the A3 event. Measurement reporting, based on SSBs but also CSI-RS, is also very important for channel estimation in terrestrial networks to aid link adaptation, primarily due to urban deployments where the various channel state and effects of multi-path propagation are highly and frequently variable and difficult to predict, except perhaps at the cell edge. In NTN deployments, on the other hand, limited multipath effects due to focus on outdoor environments, and the predictable movement of the satellite in the sky coupled with accurate weather forecast data make it such that the user link channel state by itself is much more steady and predictable, driven mostly by satellite motion, and can thus be quite reliably modelled and estimated. The overall link and HO candidate selection is, however, on the other hand, affected by a number of other factors, many of which are completely opaque to the gNB and cannot be addressed with measurements.

The gNB or Near-RT RIC monitors SMTC-configured events where signal quality exceeds a threshold while cell quality drops below another, particularly in NTN deployments where channel state is more steady due to satellite motion and weather forecast data.

text: Feeder link availability is a particularly interesting example as it is chiefly important in transparent NTN deployments where, even in FR1 user link systems, the NR-Uu waveform has to traverse also the feeder link between the satellite and the ground station, which often utilises higher frequencies \(e.g Ku, Ka-, Q- or V-band\) that are notably susceptible to weather attenuation, and which makes it such that the feeder link directly impacts the NR-Uu user link radio interface. The feeder link behavior is not specified in 3GPP, this effectively makes it opaque to the gNB. In addition, due to the dynamic nature of the system and of the external effects \(e.g. weather\) that might intervene, the impact to the NR-Uu user link introduced by the feeder link might not be completely known in advance by any of the individual gNBs at the moment of handover, due to the fact that a feeder link might not even have been established yet.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview --> 5.2.2 Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover \(HO\) due to Satellite mobility --> 5.2.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
text_preview: Feeder link availability is an interesting example in transparent NTN deployments, where the NR-Uu waveform must traverse both links between satellite and ground station. The feeder link often uses higher frequencies (e.g., Ku, Ka- or V-band) susceptible to weather attenuation, impacting the user link radio interface.

text: Continuous satellite movement also makes it such that the channel quality is, albeit predictably, always continually and steadily changing, driven effectively by gNB motion, unlike in terrestrial networks where, if the UE is stationary, the base station is in most cases static.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview --> 5.2.2 Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover \(HO\) due to Satellite mobility --> 5.2.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
text_preview: Continuous satellite movement also makes it such that the channel quality is, albeit predictably, always continually and steadily changing, driven effectively by gNB motion, unlike in terrestrial networks where, if the UE is stationary, the base station is in most cases static.

text: Not only might the different satellites and their respective feeder and user link vectors, propagating through variable weather and atmospheric conditions, result in varying channel qualities and therefore attainable MCS regimes, but they can also result in varying viable service times before either the user link or the service link becomes unsustainable, due to factors such as Line-of-Sight \(LoS\) or minimum elevation angles due to field-of-view \(FoV\) and obstructions.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview --> 5.2.2 Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover \(HO\) due to Satellite mobility --> 5.2.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
text_preview: Satellites with different feeder and user link vectors can result in varying channel qualities and MCS regimes due to weather conditions. This can also lead to varying viable service times, affected by factors such as Line-of-Sight (LoS), minimum elevation angles, and obstructions.

text: Thus, serving or neighbour cell signal measurements prior to the handover can by themselves be at least partially misleading in NTN, since they do not indicate much about either the end-to-end channel quality including the feeder link and the satellite itself \(e.g. on transparent systems\), channel state evolution throughout the satellite pass, or future vectors between each satellite and the UEs being served, or expected to be served in the future \(e.g. impacted by LoS effects, such as mountain ranges which might block LoS from a given area and UEs or feeder links to a given satellite at any future point of the service pass\). For example, for Satellite 31 in Figure 5.2.2.1-1, a feeder link is formed with a ground station in the Azores. As the satellite propagates due North-East, it may witness its current ground station fall out of view before the UE does, thus requiring a feeder link handover. While feeder link is not a 3GPP-specified element of the network, mobility procedures associated with it may still require intervention from the RAN, and, depending on network implementation, may potentially result in an L3 Handover as well for the UE, leading to potential service discontinuity and signaling overhead.

text_preview: Serving or neighbour cell signal measurements can be misleading in NTN, not indicating end-to-end channel quality or future vectors between satellites and UEs. A feeder link may require handover before the UE does, causing service discontinuity and increased signaling overhead due to mobility procedures associated with the feeder link.

text: Furthermore, since the NTN link is often more constrained compared to a terrestrial link, an excessive reliance on user link signalling and UE measurement reports may create significant overhead on the link, negatively affecting user throughput and system capacity.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview --> 5.2.2 Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover \(HO\) due to Satellite mobility --> 5.2.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
text_preview: Furthermore, since the NTN link is often more constrained compared to a terrestrial link, an excessive reliance on user link signalling and UE measurement reports may create significant overhead on the link, negatively affecting user throughput and system capacity.

text: This introduces the need for intervention, and opportunity for optimization, from an external control plane that has awareness of the satellite constellation, its sub-components and its evolution, and is thus capable of predicting the behaviour of both the user links and their channel state across multiple satellites throughout their motion, as well as the impact of components of the system that are outside of the scope of any individual gNB, such, in this example, other gNBs, other satellites or NTN service nodes, or any of the gateway feeder links. In addition, to account for events in the future impacting links that have not come into existence yet, there might be a need for the NTN control plane to be able to be spatially-aware, in addition to it being temporally-aware, to propagate predict where the NTN service nodes \(e.g. satellites, but not only\) might be at any future point in time and which links they might be able to form.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview --> 5.2.2 Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover \(HO\) due to Satellite mobility --> 5.2.2.2 Problem statement and challenges
text_preview: An external control plane with satellite constellation awareness optimizes sub-components by predicting user link behavior and channel state across multiple moving satellites and system components outside individual gNBs. To account for future events, it must be both spatially- and temporally-aware to predict service node locations and potential links.

text: 5.2.2.3 Proposed Solution
trace: 5.2.1 Overview --> 5.2.2 Use Case 2-1: Connected mode NTN inter-gNB handover \(HO\) due to Satellite mobility --> 5.2.2.3 Proposed Solution
text_preview: 5.2.2.3 Proposed Solution

text: A possible solution could be leveraging the NTN RIC, either as a combination of the Near-RT and the Non-RT RIC, or via the Near-RT RIC alone, with the introduction of a new control loop provided by one or more NTN xApp\(s\). Such xApps would leverage the holistic view of the satellite network provided by the NTN RIC, combined with predictive capabilities, to produce handover decisions which take into account multiple concurring factors, as well as reducing the reliance on signal measurements and reporting.

text: It is assumed that the NTN RIC may be capable of predicting NTN network node state, motion, trajectory \(e.g. orbit\) and behaviour in time and space. It is also assumed that the NTN RIC may be able to ingest external data sources, such as, but not limited to, weather data, to predict impact of external events on the active or candidate links, in order to aid the control loop affecting handover decisions.

text: By knowing the predictable orbital movement of the candidate satellites , their association with ground stations and feeder links, the relatively static position \(compared to the satellites\) of UE or groups of UE in a given target coverage area \(e.g. cell or cell portion\) and the impact of weather effects, an NTN xApp could drive the decision of which satellite to hand over the UE to by modelling the candidate link vectors which could be formed and sustained until the need for the next handover, and aiming to choose the one that satisfies the appropriate combination of constraints. The use of prediction can be considered a supplement to, not a replacement of the evaluation of UE measurement reports.

GoalFind best handover candidate satellites/cells for a UE to address impact of satellite motion and  
constellation evolution, while considering a number of diverse constraints and dependencies

Actors and RolesNTN xApp, Near-RT RIC, E2 Nodes, UE.

Step 1 \(M\)NTN Handover Optimization xApp/Near-RT RIC subscribes to UE information change and  
message copy of UE mobility from E2 Nodes to understand the state of the network and the  
UEs within it.  
Step 2 \(M\)NTN Handover Optimization xApp/Near-RT RIC requests to the E2 Nodes for the UEs to  
perform measurements of both serving and visible candidate target cells across satellites, and  
configure in the E2 Nodes UE information change and message copy of UE mobility to be  
reported back to the NTN Handover Optimization xApp /Near-RT RIC.  
Step 3 \(M\)E2 Nodes configure target measurements to UEs and UEs perform measurements and monitor  
for configured measurement events, upon which they signal a measurement report to the  
serving NTN E2 Node  
Step 4 \(M\)NTN E2 Nodes forward the measurement report to NTN Handover Optimization xApp/Near-RT  
RIC  
Step 5 \(M\)xApp with digital twin analyses the currently employed Ground Station and transparent LEO  
satellite to derive the remaining service time before a handover must occur. It also evaluates  
the candidate handover opportunities via available neighbouring satellites and feeder links to  
model the link performances attainable during the service times that they could respectively  
offer to the UE, and compares them with the results of the measurement reports.  
Its output is a selection of the neighbour satellite/cell which is best positioned to serve the UEs  
in the target coverage area.  
Step 6 \(M\)NTN Handover Optimization xApp/Near-RT RIC signals to NTN E2 Node to establish the  
correct handover control to the target UEs, to the selected target satellites, including the correct  
SIB19 contents \(e.g. Ephemeris\) for the respective target satellites to be included in the HO  
request message by the E2 Node.  
Step 7 \(M\)NTN E2 Node implements RRC Connected Mode handover as specified by NTN Handover  
Optimization xApp/Near-RT RIC

text: The first and main benefit is the introduction of support of Release 17+ NR NTN network-controlled Handover \(HO\) from RRC Connected Mode, including support for NTN-specific satellite assistance information in the HO request/trigger, which is presently not supported by the O-RAN specifications.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview -->  --> 5.2.2.4 Benefits
text_preview: The first and main benefit is the introduction of support of Release 17+ NR NTN network-controlled Handover \(HO\) from RRC Connected Mode, including support for NTN-specific satellite assistance information in the HO request/trigger, which is presently not supported by the O-RAN specifications.

text: The second benefit, achieved by the introduction of an NTN RIC \(Near/Non-RT RIC\) that is aware of the dynamic topology, physics and evolution of the constellation, and is capable of predicting its behaviour, is a potentially significant reduction of the signalling overhead, as well as a reduction of the potential for handover failures or sub-optimal handovers, leading to an improved service experience, as well as overall improved efficiency of the network by reduction of the resources consumed to support a mobility event.
trace: 5.2.1 Overview -->  --> 5.2.2.4 Benefits
text_preview: The introduction of an NTN RIC (Near/Non-RT RIC) aware of dynamic topology and evolution can significantly reduce signalling overhead and handover failures, leading to improved service experience and overall efficiency. This results in reduced resource consumption during mobility events, enhancing network performance.

text: The use case brings an intelligent NTN handover management approach to O-RAN, which also utilizes information that is not natively exposed by the O-RAN interfaces \(information owing to the non-3GPP components of an NTN constellation, and the constellation's own dynamic evolution.

text: There is a need to support the configuration of the previously described new measurement configurations specific to NR NTN introduced in Release 17, such as the new SSB Measurement Timing Configuration \(SMTC\) or SMTC4 \(SSB-MTC4List-r17\). In addition, the NTN cells must be able to broadcast Satellite Assistance information, in particular Satellite Ephemeris, in the form of SIB19, containing serving and neighbor satellite and cell information. Furthermore, in order to trigger a HO, the gNB must be able to include specific SIB19 content in the HO triggers.

These cells must broadcast Satellite Assistance information (SIB19) containing serving and neighbor satellite and cell info. To trigger a Handover (HO), the gNB must include specific SIB19 content in HO triggers.
